To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Umayyads used glass tesserae of Byzantine and Byzantine-style manufacture in their mosaics; (2) the Umayys were also able to produce their own glass tesserae; (3) the production of glass tesseraes in the Umayad period was not limited to mosaics but also included the production of glass vessels.
the Umayyads used glass tesserae made in Egypt and in the Levant in their mosaic pavements, and that they also used glass vessels made in Egypt, the Levant and possibly in Byzantine workshops.

the analysis of glass tesseraes from the qasrs of Khirbet Mafjar and Khirbet al-Samra (Jericho, West Bank, Palestine), and of glass vessels from the qasar of Khirbet el-Mafjar, revealed that both the mosaic tesseraes and glass vessels were produced in Egypt and the Syrio–Palestinian coast.

the study of a material culture that has a crucial role in the definition and understanding of the Byzantine-Islamic transition in the near East, which has been so far mainly studied through written sources and archaeological data.
the study of the transition between the Byzantine and the Islamic periods, with particular attention to the effects of the Islamic conquest on the glass industry in the Levant.
the analysis of the material culture of the Umayyads, with the aim of understanding the cultural transition that occurred between the Byzantine and the early Islamic periods.

the Byzantine–Umayyad transition did not affect the supply of glass in the Levant and that the Islamic period did not witness a radical change in the glassware production and consumption.
the Byzantine–Arab transition in the Near East was not as sudden as previously thought, but it was characterised by a long-lasting and complex process.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Umayyads were able to maintain the Byzantine glass production tradition and to continue to use the same glass sources, while at the same time they were able to introduce new glass compositions, possibly from Egypt.
the Byzantine–Umayyad transition in the Near East was not as clear as it was thought, at least in terms of glass production and consumption.
the Byzantine–Muslim transition was not a sharp break in the production and use of glass in Palestine and the Levant, as it has been commonly believed.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the transition from the Byzantine to the Islamic period in the Levant is not as abrupt as it has been traditionally thought and that the Byzantines and the Byzantine glassware manufacture did not disappear from the Levant after the Islamic conquests.
glass tesserae are a valuable source of information to understand the effects of the transition from the Byzantine to the Islamic rule on the glass industry in the near East.
